title: Isothermal cross-priming amplification for field-deployable norovirus surveillance: a cost-effective and rapid solution.
abstract: ABSTRACT Norovirus remains a leading cause of foodborne gastroenteritis globally. While isothermal amplification technologies offer advantages over traditional reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) in terms of speed and portability, there is a lack of domestically developed isothermal amplification systems for norovirus in China. Using a domestic patented cross-priming amplification (CPA) technology, we established CPA systems targeting the predominant norovirus genotypes GII.3, GII.4, and GII.17. The systems were evaluated using 224 fecal samples with confirmed genotypes via sequencing. Our lab-developed CPA (Lab-CPA) systems demonstrated high sensitivity, detecting 98.0% (49/50) of GII.3, 100% (80/80) of GII.4, and 96.9% (31/32) of GII.17 samples, with 100% specificity across all genotypes. Compared to certified clinical RT-qPCR kits, the total percent agreement was 98.7%, 99.3%, and 96.9% for GII.3, GII.4, and GII.17, respectively, accompanied by a significant linear correlation in threshold times. Crucially, the Lab-CPA systems reduced processing time by 44–60 min compared to RT-qPCR. Successful integration into the commercial EasyNAT platform using all-in-one cartridges further streamlined the workflow while maintaining accuracy. Our CPA systems offer a rapid, cost-effective, and streamlined diagnostic solution, ideally suited for point-of-care testing in resource-limited primary healthcare environments. IMPORTANCE Norovirus remains a critical public health threat, driving demand for rapid, deployable diagnostics. While isothermal amplification offers theoretical advantages over reverse transcription quantitative PCR, the absence of domestically developed systems in China has created a reliance on imported assays, limiting point-of-care testing capabilities. This study addresses that gap by establishing a novel cross-priming amplification system tailored to China’s predominant norovirus genotypes. Achieving high sensitivity/specificity and significantly reducing processing time, this work validates a robust, field-adaptable alternative to conventional methods. Furthermore, successful integration with the commercial EasyNAT platform demonstrates immediate translational potential. By providing a cost-effective, high-performance domestic solution, these findings significantly enhance decentralized surveillance and emergency response capacity for norovirus infections in resource-limited settings.

title: Ultrasound-Treated Ethanolic Extracts of Endemic Mount Ida Plants (Sideritis trojana and Hypericum kazdaghensis) Show Antiviral and Antibacterial Potential Against Norovirus Surrogates and Foodborne Bacteria.
abstract: Human noroviruses and persistent bacterial pathogens remain major food-safety concerns. This screening study compared 40% (v/v) ethanolic extracts (EE) and ultrasound-treated ethanolic extracts (UTE) of the endemic Mount Ida plants Sideritis trojana Ehrend. and Hypericum kazdaghensis Gemici & Leblebici. Feline calicivirus (FCV) and murine norovirus (MNV) served as cultivable human-norovirus surrogates; four reference bacteria were examined by disc diffusion. Ultrasound treatment was associated with higher measured total phenolic content (approximately 2.2- to 3.8-fold) and antioxidant capacity (approximately 1.9- to 2.3-fold) than EE. The largest reduction was 4.71 log 10 TCID 50 /mL for H. kazdaghensis-UTE against FCV after overnight exposure. For MNV, the largest reduction was 2.42 log 10 TCID 50 /mL for S. trojana-EE after overnight exposure. Inhibition-zone diameters ranged from 6.25 to 11.75 mm, including the 6-mm disc. FRhK-4 viability ranged from approximately 56% to 100% across the tested conditions, precluding a general claim of low cytotoxicity. The results provide preliminary, surrogate- and assay-specific evidence of antiviral and antibacterial activity. Because solvent-only and positive controls were not included, causal attribution to plant constituents and comparison with established antimicrobials are not possible. Confirmatory controlled assays are required before practical food-safety use can be proposed.

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: Human noroviruses and persistent bacterial pathogens remain major food-safety concerns. This study aimed to evaluate the antiviral and antibacterial potential of plant extracts against norovirus surrogates and foodborne bacteria.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: A screening study was conducted to compare 40% (v/v) ethanolic extracts (EE) and ultrasound-treated ethanolic extracts (UTE) of the endemic Mount Ida plants Sideritis trojana Ehrend and Hypericum kazdaghensis Gemici & Leblebici. analysis_en.methods: The study used feline calicivirus (FCV) and murine norovirus (MNV) as cultivable human-norovirus surrogates and tested four reference bacteria using disc diffusion. The results provide preliminary, surrogate- and assay-specific evidence of antiviral and antibacterial activity.
analysis_en.main_results: Ultrasound treatment was associated with higher measured total phenolic content (approximately 2.2- to 3.8-fold) and antioxidant capacity (approximately 1.9- to 2.3-fold) than EE. analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The results suggest that ultrasound-treated extracts may enhance antiviral properties compared to ethanolic extracts. However, the study emphasizes the need for confirmatory controlled assays before practical food-safety applications can be proposed.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings may inform future research on natural antiviral agents for food safety, particularly in the context of norovirus surrogates and bacterial pathogens. analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Because solvent-only and positive controls were not included, causal attribution to plant constituents and comparison with established antimicrobials are not possible. title: Hydroxyl Radical Inactivation of Vesicle-Cloaked and Free Murine Norovirus: Linking Biomolecular Oxidation to Lifecycle Disruption and Infectivity Loss.
abstract: Hydroxyl radicals (•OH) play a central role in inactivating human viruses during advanced oxidation processes for water and wastewater treatment, solar disinfection, and natural attenuation in sunlit aquatic environments. Human norovirus, a leading cause of gastroenteritis, is efficiently transmitted through water and exhibits strong environmental persistence. The recent discovery of vesicle-cloaked virus clusters (viral vesicles) further challenges water treatment and reuse, particularly for norovirus elimination. We investigated •OH inactivation kinetics and mechanisms of murine norovirus 1 (MNV-1), a human norovirus surrogate, in free-virus and vesicle-cloaked forms. •OH rapidly inactivated both MNV-1 vesicles and free MNV-1 with second rate constants of ∼1010 M-1 s-1; however, the vesicle membrane provided a 2.24-fold protective effect to cloaked MNV-1, resulting in slower inactivation kinetics than those of free MNV-1. •OH oxidized viral capsid proteins and genomes together with vesicle proteins and lipids, resulting in impaired CD300lf receptor and cell-based binding, disrupted genome replication, and diminished viral assembly. Despite these biochemical and functional impairments, most vesicle structures remained largely intact following •OH exposure. This study establishes a quantitative framework linking biomolecular damage to viral infectivity loss through functional impairment and lifecycle disruption, providing mechanistic insights into advance water disinfection strategies and public health protection.

title: Association between glycerin enema use and 14-day unplanned revisits in children with acute viral gastroenteritis: a dual-center retrospective cohort study
abstract: Abstract Background Glycerin enema is commonly used in pediatric emergency settings to relieve fecal impaction, yet evidence on its effect on short-term outcomes in acute viral gastroenteritis remains scarce. This study examined the association between glycerin enema administered within 12 hours of initial presentation and the 14-day unplanned revisit rate in children with rotavirus- and/or norovirus-induced acute viral gastroenteritis. Methods This dual-center retrospective cohort study enrolled children aged ≤ 14 years with positive stool antigen for rotavirus and/or norovirus at Dongguan Tungwah Hospital and Dongguan Songshan Lake Tungwah Hospital from January 2021 to August 2025. Propensity score matching (PSM) was performed using exact matching on non-diarrhea presentation status, followed by 1∶1 nearest-neighbor matching without replacement based on standardized Euclidean distance for gender, age in months, intravenous fluid administration, and fever. The primary outcome was the 14-day unplanned revisit rate, analyzed by paired McNemar exact test. Secondary outcomes included antibiotic use, hospitalization, and symptom duration ≥ 3 days. Sensitivity analyses included Firth penalized logistic regression, exclusion of hospitalized children, and E-value assessment. Results PSM yielded 178 well-balanced pairs, with all five covariates achieving SMD

title: Epidemiological features and direct medical costs of norovirus acute gastroenteritis in China
abstract: Norovirus is a leading global cause of acute gastroenteritis (AGE), yet comprehensive data on its disease and economic burden across all age groups requiring medical consultation in China remains scarce, hindering evidence-based public health strategy formulation. A multi-center retrospective study was conducted on 23,527 AGE patients who underwent norovirus testing at medical institutions in four Chinese provinces between 2018 and 2024. The logistic regression models were used to analyze the related factors with norovirus infection rates, hospitalization risks, complication incidence, and direct medical costs. National annual direct medical burden of norovirus infection was estimated by combining study data with national population census and epidemiological survey data. The overall norovirus positive rate was 18.80% (95% CI 18.30%-19.30%), with a significantly higher rate in inpatients (26.15%, 95% CI 25.28%-27.04%) than outpatients (13.78%, 95% CI 13.21%-14.36%). Children < 5 years old had the highest positive rate (30.49%, 95% CI 29.56%-31.43%. A total of 18.97% (95% CI 17.84%–20.16%) of norovirus-positive patients developed at least one potential complication concurrent with norovirus-positive acute gastroenteritis, among which dehydration (11.28%, 95% CI 10.39%–12.25%) was the most prevalent, followed by convulsions (5.52%, 95% CI 4.88%–6.23%). The median direct medical costs for inpatients (CNY 4,580, IQR 3,129–6,402) was far higher than outpatients (CNY 230 IQR 128–354), with the elderly ≥ 65 years having the highest per capita direct medical costs (CNY 5,322, IQR 2,411–10,798). The national annual direct medical cost of norovirus infection was estimated at CNY 20.23 billion, with children < 5 years bearing a medical burden 11.2 times that of the elderly ≥ 60 years. Norovirus infection among hospital-tested patients in China exhibits the disparities in disease burden by age, region and season. Children aged < 5 years tended to experience more severe clinical manifestations, whereas patients aged ≥ 65 years appeared to bear higher individual medical expenditure in our hospital-based samples. Age-targeted public health strategies and regionally tailored healthcare resource allocation are urgently needed to address the heterogeneous disease burden of norovirus infection in China.

title: Application of VirCapSeq-VERT for viral pathogen detection in children under five with acute diarrheal illness in Zambia
abstract: Diarrheal disease remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality among children under five years, especially in low- and middle-income countries, particularly sub-Saharan Africa. Although rotavirus vaccination has reduced burden in children, a substantial proportion of diarrhea remains unattributed due to limited diagnostic capacity. We applied VirCapSeq-VERT (VCS), a virome-wide targeted sequencing technique, to characterize viral detections and co-infection patterns in stool samples from children with diarrhea and to explore their comparison with disease severity. A cross-sectional, facility-based study across nine provincial health facilities in Zambia. Stool collected from children U5 years presenting with diarrhea was analyzed using qPCR and VCS. Positivity by VCS was defined as ≥ 25% in relation to full coding reference sequence. Severity was assessed using the Vesikari scoring system and categorized as mild or moderate-to-severe. Descriptive and comparative analyses were performed to evaluate viral prevalence, age-specific distribution, and co-infection patterns. Samples from 247 participants were analyzed by VCS with 48.6% aged 0–12 months; males accounting for 52.6%. Using VCS to interrogate the stool samples, rotavirus A was the most detected virus (42.5%), followed by enterovirus (36%), human herpesvirus (HHV) (30%), adenovirus (25.5%), astrovirus (23.9%), and norovirus (22.7%). VCS detected a broader range of viral pathogens among the subset of 233 participant samples that were also tested using qPCR, with higher prevalence measurements for adenovirus (24.5% by VCS vs. 10.7% by qPCR) and norovirus (21.9% by VCS vs. 15.9% by qPCR) whereas rotavirus A and astrovirus showed comparable prevalence across both platforms. Age-specific trends revealed decreasing prevalence of rotavirus with increasing age, while adenovirus and enterovirus predominated in children aged > 24 months. No individual viral pathogen was significantly associated with diarrhea severity; however, rotavirus co-infections modified outcomes, with rotavirus-sapovirus associated with increased severity (aPR = 1.39, 95% CI 1.03–1.88, p = 0.029). Dual infections were common (31.9%), while mono-infections accounted for 38.5% of cases, and 8.9% had no detectable virus. VCS enables broad detection of pathogenic viruses, revealing diversity and co-infections in pediatric diarrheal disease. Expanded viral surveillance may improve pathogen detection, guide clinical management, reduce inappropriate antibiotic use, assess vaccine strategies, and strengthen disease control in high-burden settings.

title: Evolution, diversity and distribution of human Noroviruses:From single hosts to global patterns
abstract: Norovirus, a member of the Caliciviridae family, is a major cause of acute gastroenteritis (AGE) worldwide, affecting all age groups and causing substantial morbidity and mortality. Children in developing countries, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals are particularly affected. Currently, no specific antivirals or vaccines are licensed for norovirus treatment or prevention. Therapeutic development is complicated by the virus's high diversity, with more than 10 genogroups (GI–GX) and approximately 50 genotypes, some of which, such as GII.4, continuously generate new antigenic variants. However, the emergence of norovirus diversity, the relationship between within-host and community-level evolution, and the association between viral diversity and treatment outcome remain incompletely understood. Therefore, this thesis aims to improve our understanding of norovirus evolution and epidemiology by addressing two main topics: norovirus diversity and evolution in different hosts, and the use of wastewater-based sequencing to monitor viral diversity and circulation at the population level.

title: Molecular Detection of Gastrointestinal Pathogens Using a Multiplex Gastrointestinal Panel and Their Associations With Demographic and Clinical Characteristics
abstract: BackgroundAcute gastroenteritis causes morbidity across all age groups, and timely, effective identification of its etiologic agents is essential for clinical management and antimicrobial stewardship.Conventional diagnostic methods have limited sensitivity and often fail to detect coinfections or specific bacterial pathotypes.In contrast, molecular methods, such as FilmArray panels, are rapid, highly sensitive, and capable of detecting coinfections.This study aimed to characterize gastrointestinal pathogens detected by the BioFire FilmArray Gastrointestinal Panel (BioFire Diagnostics, LLC, Salt Lake City, UT, USA; a bioMérieux company) and to evaluate their association with demographic and clinical characteristics among patients at Hospital Angeles Lindavista, Mexico City, Mexico. MethodsA retrospective observational study conducted from January 2022 to July 2025 included all patients who underwent gastrointestinal molecular testing.Demographic data, clinical characteristics, and multiplex PCR results were extracted from electronic medical records and the FilmArray database.Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, logistic regression, Fisher's exact test, and Spearman correlation. ResultsAn analysis of 1,120 samples found an overall positivity rate of 906 (81%).Coinfections were present in 543 (49%) cases.The most common pathogens were enteropathogenic Escherichia coli (E.coli, EPEC; 374, 33.4%); enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC; 281, 25.1%); and enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC; 231, 20.6%).Rotavirus A (206, 18.4%) and norovirus GI/GII (168, 15%) were the most frequent.Positivity was highest in children under five (147, 84.48%) and lowest in adults over 60 (129, 73.71%).Seasonal patterns showed unexpected peaks of rotavirus in spring-summer and of Cyclospora cayetanensis in summer.No significant association was found between pathogen presence and comorbidities, likely due to many missing clinical details.A negative correlation among major E. coli pathotypes suggests competitive exclusion. ConclusionThe BioFire FilmArray Gastrointestinal Panel identified pathogen patterns that conventional methods miss.Age and seasonal trends highlight the need for localized epidemiological surveillance.These results encourage the use of molecular diagnostics in routine assessments of gastrointestinal infections and support antimicrobial stewardship efforts.Future studies should include clinical severity metrics and evaluate patient outcomes to connect molecular detection with clinical significance.

Rotavirus A (206, 18.4%) and norovirus GI/GII (168, 15%) were the most frequent. Positivity was highest in children under five (147, 84.48%) and lowest in adults over 60 (129, 73.71%). A retrospective observational study conducted from January 2022 to July 2025 included all patients who underwent gastrointestinal molecular testing. Demographic data, clinical characteristics, and multiplex PCR results were extracted from electronic medical records and the FilmArray database. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, logistic regression, Fisher’s exact test, and Spearman correlation. Acute gastroenteritis causes morbidity across all age groups, and timely, effective identification of its etiologic agents is essential for clinical management and antimicrobial stewardship. Conventional diagnostic methods have limited sensitivity and often fail to detect coinfections or specific bacterial pathotypes. In contrast, molecular methods, such as FilmArray panels, are rapid, highly sensitive, and capable of detecting coinfections. This study aimed to characterize gastrointestinal pathogens detected by the BioFire FilmArray Gastrointestinal Panel (BioFire Diagnostics, LLC, Salt Lake City, UT, USA; a bioMérieux company) and to evaluate their association with demographic and clinical characteristics among patients at Hospital Angeles Lindavista, Mexico City, Mexico. Introduction Gastrointestinal infections are a common reason for seeking medical care and a global public health problem. While pediatric patients are known to be the most vulnerable, these infections also represent a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in adults, particularly those with comorbidities [1,2]. Rapid, timely diagnosis improves treatment, disease course, and prognosis and supports epidemiological surveillance. One of the greatest challenges in establishing a diagnosis is the wide range of pathogens that can cause infection, including viruses, bacteria, and parasites, acting alone or in combination [3]. Current diagnostic testing options include culture, staining, and antigen detection. These methods may require collecting multiple samples, involve extensive sample preparation, and have low sensitivity and prolonged turnaround times. Traditionally, the gold standard for microbiological diagnosis includes culture for Salmonella spp., Shigella spp., Campylobacter, and Escherichia coli (E. coli), as well as rapid tests for rotavirus. However, these agents account for only 25%-30% of diarrheal syndromes [4]. Molecular detection tests have expanded the capacity to detect pathogens. However, their availability is limited for most of the population due to their high cost and limited access in public health institutions [5]. For the FilmArray Gastrointestinal Panel, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has validated its clinical use, allowing detection in a single reaction of 22 enteric pathogens (13 bacteria, five viruses, and four parasites) and resistance genes [6]. In Mexico, this technique is not widely available in public health services and is used only in specific cases or in the private sector [7]. Therefore, describing its use in the general population is relevant, as is its association with clinical characteristics such as diagnosis, comorbidities, and risk factors. This study aims to identify and describe the microorganisms detected in patients who underwent a gastrointestinal molecular panel at Hospital Ángeles Lindavista, Mexico City, Mexico, from January 2022 to July 2025, without establishing a definitive cause-and-effect relationship, and to evaluate their correlation with demographic and clinical features. To this end, we will conduct a retrospective, descriptive analysis, with the results intended to inform improvements in patient care, diagnosis, treatment, antimicrobial stewardship decisions, and epidemiological surveillance. Materials & Methods Study design We conducted a retrospective, observational, cross-sectional study at Hospital Angeles Lindavista from January 2022 to July 2025. Its goal was to identify and examine gastrointestinal pathogens, including bacteria, viruses, and parasites, detected by the BioFire FilmArray Gastrointestinal Panel (BioFire Diagnostics, LLC, Salt Lake City, UT, USA; a bioMérieux company). The study aimed not only to understand epidemiological patterns but also to associate these pathogens with patients' demographic and clinical features; it included all patients who received a gastrointestinal molecular panel, whether as outpatients or while hospitalized. Analyzed variables included demographics, patient type, comorbidities, risk factors, diagnoses, detected pathogens, and infection type. Data sources included the FilmArray multiplex PCR system database (by bioMérieux) and the Hospital Angeles Lindavista Electronic Clinical History (ECH) database. Laboratory testing Samples examined were stool specimens. We identified gastrointestinal pathogens using the BioFire FilmArray Gastrointestinal Panel multiplex PCR system. This certified device combines nucleic acid extraction, reverse transcription, first-stage multiplex PCR, and second-stage nested PCR within a single disposable pouch. It employs freeze-dried reagents and multiple primers optimized for a common annealing temperature, allowing simultaneous qualitative detection of 22 gastrointestinal pathogens, such as diarrheagenic E. coli types, Campylobacter, Salmonella, Vibrio, Yersinia enterocolitica, Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) toxin A/B, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia, adenovirus F40/41, astrovirus, norovirus GI/GII, rotavirus A, and sapovirus. All steps occur inside sealed blister compartments in the pouch, reducing manual handling and contamination risk and delivering results in about an hour. We performed tests following the manufacturer's protocols. Results labeled "detected" or "not detected" were considered valid. If a process failed, we marked the result "invalid" and repeated the test. This approach improves diagnostic speed and helps detect coinfections but has limitations: sensitivity varies among targets; it does not quantify microbial load, so it cannot differentiate active infection from colonization or residual nucleic acids, and it detects only organisms within the panel and cannot identify pathogens outside it. A negative result does not rule out microorganisms not among the panel's targets. Therefore, we interpreted results alongside clinical presentation and additional diagnostics. Data source We compiled a retrospective database from Hospital Angeles Lindavista for the specified period, including data from 1,120 patients. We de-identified the patients' data and standardized and grouped variable coding for analysis. Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were conducted using R version 4.5.1 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) in RStudio (Posit Software, PBC, Boston, MA, USA). Descriptive Analysis Categorical variables were summarized with their absolute counts and percentages. For the continuous variable (age), we assessed the data distribution and reported the mean and standard deviation (SD). Overall and age-specific positivity rates were calculated by dividing detected cases by the total samples processed. Seasonality Analysis We examined the monthly detection frequency of the top 10 most common pathogens over the study period (2022-2025) to identify seasonal trends and periodic fluctuations. Inferential Analysis and Associations To analyze links between clinical variables (such as comorbidities and risk factors) and pathogen presence, we used binary logistic regression to calculate odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). For small subgroups (n < 5), we used Fisher's exact test for sensitivity checks. Finally, to investigate microbial interactions (coinfections versus mutual exclusion), we created a correlation matrix based on Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, considering only statistically significant interactions. All statistical tests used a significance threshold of p < 0.05 (two-tailed). Ethical considerations The Research Ethics Committee of Hospital Angeles Pedregal approved the study protocol (approval number: HAP 2786). All procedures followed the ethical standards outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. The committee granted a waiver of informed consent for this retrospective study because of its minimal-risk design. Confidentiality and data protection were maintained throughout the study. Results Characteristics of the study population A total of 1,120 samples from patients with suspected gastrointestinal infection treated at Hospital Angeles Lindavista between January 2022 and July 2025 were analyzed. The mean age of the patients was 33.6 years (SD ± 23.1). A balanced gender distribution was observed, with 616 (55%) female patients. Most samples (1,028, 92%) were from hospitalized patients, while 92 (8%) were from outpatients (Table 1). For the age variable, the values correspond to the mean and standard deviation (SD). For the other values, these correspond to the number of cases (n) and the percentage of the total population (%). Regarding the diagnosis, 878 (79%) patients were admitted with acute gastroenteritis, 74 (6.6%) with gastroenteritis secondary to C. difficile, and 28 (2.5%) had no reported diagnosis. In 761 (68%) and 709 (64%) of the analyzed population, the presence of comorbidities and risk factors was unknown, respectively. Among patients with available information, hypertension (48, 4.3%) and diabetes (41, 3.7%) were the most frequent comorbidities, while immunosuppression (27, 2.4%) and the presence of concomitant infections (15, 1.3%) were among the most common risk factors (Table 2). Among positive cases, coinfections were common: 363 (32%) had single infections (one pathogen), while 543 (49%) had multiple infections (two, three, or more than four pathogens detected simultaneously) (Table 3). Each pair of data points corresponds to the number of cases (n) and the percentage of the total population (%). Pathogenic bacteria dominated the microbiological profile. Conversely, adults over 60 years had the lowest detection rate at 129/175 (73.71%), suggesting a potentially higher prevalence of non-infectious or undetectable causes in this age group. Adults aged 18 to 59 show a slightly lower rate of 502/619 (81.1%), while those over 60 have the lowest rate at 129/175 (73.71%). These data suggest that positivity decreases with age, highlighting age-related differences in detecting the pathogen. Seasonality patterns Monthly trend analysis revealed seasonal patterns (Figure 3). Unlike the common winter peaks seen elsewhere, rotavirus detections surged in spring and summer (March-June), aligning with peaks in bacterial pathogens such as Salmonella spp. and various E. coli strains. Furthermore, C. difficile cases peaked from May to July. Cyclospora cayetanensis also showed a distinct summer seasonal pattern. title: National trends in pathogen-specific diagnoses and outcomes among hospitalizations for infectious diarrhea.
abstract: BACKGROUND: The diagnostic evaluation of infectious diarrhea has evolved with increasing adoption of multiplex gastrointestinal nucleic acid amplification tests and changing diagnostic strategies for Clostridioides difficile. OBJECTIVES: We aimed to assess changes in inpatient pathogen-specific documentation rates and clinical outcomes on a national level. METHODS: We performed a retrospective cross-sectional study using the National Inpatient Sample from 2016 to 2023. Adult hospitalizations with a primary diagnosis of presumed infectious diarrhea were identified using ICD-10 codes. Temporal trends in pathogen-specific documentation were evaluated. Multivariable regression models were used to identify factors associated with pathogen-specific documentation and evaluate associations with clinical outcomes. RESULTS: A total of 1,174,500 hospitalizations for presumed infectious diarrhea were identified, of which 710,335 (60.5%) had a specified pathogen. Pathogen specification rates remained stable from 2016 to 2023 (minimum of 59.6% in 2019 to the maximum of 62.1% in 2023; OR per year 1.00, 95% CI: 1.00-1.01, p = .282). Clostridioides difficile declined over time, accounting for 53.7% of infectious diarrhea hospitalizations in 2016 compared to 41.2% in 2023 (OR per year 0.94, p < .001). In contrast, norovirus and Campylobacter jejuni increased during the study period. Older age and higher comorbidity burden were independently associated with increased pathogen-specific documentation. Pathogen-specific documentation was associated with increased mortality (aOR 3.15, 95% CI: 2.73-3.63). These associations were substantially attenuated after exclusion of Clostridioides difficile. CONCLUSIONS: Pathogen-specific documentation rates among hospitalizations for presumed infectious diarrhea remained stable nationally from 2016 to 2023, although identification of non-Clostridioides difficile infections appeared to increase.
